First of all, let's import the `pipeline()` function from the `transformers` library. `transformers` provides access to several *deep learning models* for NLP and speech processing hosted on <a href="https://huggingface.co/" target="_blank">HuggingFace</a>. The `pipeline()` function provides a very simple interface to access these models and apply them to common tasks (e.g., text generation, transcription of audio, predict missing word).

```{python}
from transformers import pipeline
```

## Text Generation

Transformer models like GPT-2 are **pretrained to generate natural language based on linguistic prompts** (we all know *chatGPT*!). Unlike newer GPT versions, *GPT-2* has been made freely available via *HuggingFace*, and it can be used even without an openAI API and any billing plan. All we have to do is initialize and use an instance of `pipeline()` with required task as `"text-generation"` and the desired model (`"gpt2"`).

::: cell
```{python, cache=T}
textgenerator = pipeline(
    task="text-generation", 
    model="gpt2"
)

text = textgenerator("Once upon a time in academia", max_new_tokens=150, temperature=1)

print(text)
```

<style> pre, code { white-space: pre-wrap; word-break: break-word; } </style>
:::

The model continues the text following the initial prompt that you provided with a series of plausible (even though not necessarily coherent) sentences. In addition to the *prompt*, we have passed two arguments:

-   `max_new_tokens`, which defines the maximum number of tokens in the generated sequence;
-   `temperature` which controls the randomness of predictions: lower values make the output more deterministic and even repetitive, while higher values leads to more randomness and creativity, but at extreme values may lead to totally incoherent outputs (`temperature` must be greater than `0` and smaller than `2`).

If you want to use more state-of-the-art models, you can turn to the OpenAI API, but note that to do so you need **a valid** billing plan and have created **a valid API key** (also, the following code may no longer work if OpenAI changes the pipeline interface, which happens quite often):

``` python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key="sk-proj-4slS9XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX")

response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-5.5",
    input="Once upon a time in academia"
)

generated_text = response.output_text
```

## Audio Speech Transcription

Another very useful application is automatic **speech recognition and transcription**. In the following chunk we use a *whisper* model to transcribe a short speech from an `.mp3` file

The specific model we use here (`"openai/whisper-small"`), which is quite lightweight, can be found on *HuggingFace* at this link: <a href="https://huggingface.co/openai/whisper-small" target="_blank">https://huggingface.co/openai/whisper-small</a>. Larger and more powerful versions, like `"openai/whisper-medium"` and `"openai/whisper-large"` are also available

::: cell
```{python, cache=T}
#| messages: false
#| warnings: false
whisperpipe = pipeline(model="openai/whisper-small")

transcription = whisperpipe("data/gelmanstats.mp3", return_timestamps=True)

print(transcription['text'])
```

<style> pre, code { white-space: pre-wrap; word-break: break-word; } </style>
:::

-   ⚠️ Download the audio file <a href="data/gelmanstats.mp3" Download>`gelmanstats.mp3`</a>, and then make sure that it can be correctly accessed from the working directory.
-   `return_timestamps=True` is required for relatively long audios, but it can be set to `False` for shorter audios for a simpler output.

If you prefer not to download and run the whole `whisper` model locally, you could use the OpenAI API (this effectively transfers the task on the cloud). But note that to do so you need **a valid** <a href="https://platform.openai.com/settings/organization/billing/overview" target="_blank">billing plan with OpenAI</a> and **a valid API key** (also, the following code may no longer work if OpenAI changes the pipeline interface, which happens quite often):

``` python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key="sk-proj-4slS9XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX")

audio_file = open("data/gelmanstats.mp3", "rb")

transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
    model="whisper-1",
    file = audio_file
)
print(transcript)
```

## Predict Missing Word

Models like BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) are trained to predict sentences and tokens that follow in a text. An interest feature is that they allow to to **predict a missing "masked" word** in a chunk of text, based on the surrounding context. This can be adapted for tasks like establishing the most expected word in a context, correcting typos or clarifying the meaning of ambiguous sentences given the context.

The specific model we use here can be found on *HuggingFace* at this link: <a href="https://huggingface.co/google-bert/bert-base-uncased" target="_blank">https://huggingface.co/google-bert/bert-base-uncased</a>

```{python, cache=T}
findmaskedword = pipeline(
    task="fill-mask", 
    model="bert-base-uncased"
)

findmaskedword("My professor is [MASK].")
```

We get the top 5 most likely words for the masked token. To demonstrate how the likelihood of the words change with the context, let's slightly modify the sentence:

```{python, cache=T}
findmaskedword("My professor is [MASK], so don't worry.")
```

## Image Classification

Let's try a simple example of **image classification** using a pretrained computer vision model from *HuggingFace*. The chosen model (`"microsoft/resnet-18"`)is not very powerful, but it is small and very lightweight (for more powerful but also heavier model, try`"microsoft/resnet-152"`, `"google/efficientnet-b4"` or `"google/efficientnet-b7"`). The task is to predict the most likely category for the image below

<img src="data/figureexample.png" width="600" height="auto"/>

```{python, cache=T}
#| messages: false
#| warnings: false

from PIL import Image
myImage = Image.open("data/figureexample.png")

imageclassifier = pipeline(
    task="image-classification", 
    model="microsoft/resnet-18"
)

predictions = imageclassifier(myImage)
print(predictions)
```

## Sentiment Analysis

Sentiment analysis is a typical example of **text classification**. The model receives a short text and predicts its emotional tone.

The default Hugging Face sentiment model is (now) binary: it classifies texts as either just `POSITIVE` or `NEGATIVE` (with the `score` being the confidence, not the emotional intensity). This can be misleading when a sentence is neutral, ambiguous, or mixed. For example, `"The service was okay, nothing special"` is not clearly negative, but a binary model is forced to choose one of the two available labels.

For this reason, we use here a model that includes three sentiment categories: `negative`, `neutral`, and `positive`.

```{python, cache=T}
#| messages: false
#| warnings: false

# Load a pre-trained sentiment analysis model
classifier = pipeline(
    task="sentiment-analysis",
    model="cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment-latest"
)

# Test the model with some example text
texts = [
    "I absolutely love this product! It's amazing.",
    "This is the worst experience I've ever had.",
    "The service was okay.",
    "The movie was neither great nor terrible, just average.",
    "Will you take other courses after this one?"
]
# Run sentiment analysis
results = classifier(texts)
results
```

## Text Classification

*Sentiment analysis* is a special case of a more general task: **text classification**. In text classification, the model assigns each text to **one or more predefined categories**. These categories may represent whatever (different topics, emotions, intentions, clinical risk indicators, or any other labels, provided they existed in the model training set...).

A particularly flexible option is **zero-shot classification**. We provide a list of candidate labels, and the model estimates which label best describes each text. This can be useful for exploratory work, classification of open-ended answers, etc.

```{python, cache=T}
#| messages: false
#| warnings: false

zeroshot = pipeline(
    task="zero-shot-classification",
    model="typeform/distilbert-base-uncased-mnli"
)

texts = [
    "I felt proud after finishing a task that seemed impossible at first.",
    "I could not sleep because I kept thinking about tomorrow's exam.",
    "I enjoy solving difficult puzzles and trying new strategies.",
    "I felt lonely even though I was surrounded by other people.",
    "I missed having someone to talk to after moving to a new city.",
    "I was worried that I would make a mistake in front of everyone.",
    "I feel excited when I make progress on a challenging problem."
]

candidate_labels = [
    "anxiety",
    "motivation",
    "loneliness"
]

classification_results = zeroshot(texts, candidate_labels)

classification_results
```

## *What could you do next?*

-   Play a bit with text generation and change the prompt (e.g., `"In the far future,"`, `"Brilliant psychologists discovered that"`)
-   Vary arguments like `max_length`, `num_return_sequences`, or `temperature` and see what happens to text generation.
-   Try to run image classification using pictures with different styles (e.g., photographs, drawings) and see the performance of the model.
-   If you have a few pictures of different categories (e.g., *animate objects* vs *inanimate objects*), try to run a look, classify all of them, and then use another model for text classification to categorize the textual outputs into these two (or more) *a priori* categories.
-   Have a look at all `task` options that are available using *transformers pipelines*, at this link: <a href="https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/pipelines" target="_blank">https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/pipelines</a> (e.g., try `text-classification`, `"zero-shot-classification"`, `translation` using the *`"Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-it"`* model for English-to-Italian translation).
